UGC BEAT SHEET: [Brand] SPF 50 sunscreen stick, Rs 499
Instagram Reels partnership ad | creator: 24-year-old Pune college student

BRIEF HEADER
Product: [Brand] sunscreen stick, Rs 499. One message: sunscreen that goes on without a white face.
Viewer: Pune two-wheeler commuters, 18-30, who skip sunscreen because it feels messy.
Format: 30 s, 9:16, phone-shot, sound on with captions, natural light, no filter on skin.
Tone: desi casual Roman Hinglish, "tum" register. Rewrite freely.
Must-say, exact: "SPF 50, no white cast." Brand holds the proof: [SPF test report ref], [no-white-cast test summary]. Show it on your own skin.
Must-not-say: "tan nahi hoga", "sunburn-proof", "waterproof", "dermat-approved", competitor names, any result in "X din". Say "[X] din se try kiya" only with your real number.
Disclosure: label "Ad" plus "Paid partnership with [Brand]" on screen from 0:00, held at least 10 s (a third of 30 s). Instagram's Paid partnership tag on. Caption starts "Ad". Free product? Say so.
Deliverables: 4 hooks x 1 body. A 15 s cut (hook, demo, CTA) is fine; changes to your words need your OK.

HOOK OPTIONS (product in hand from frame 1)
Hook 1, POV: "POV: Karve Road, 2 baje ki dhoop." Visual: red light, you squint, pull the stick from your jacket pocket. Text: "POV: Pune, 2 baje ka signal".
Hook 2: "Sunscreen lagaya aur chehra chalk ban gaya?" Visual: helmet off at the college gate, stick in hand. Text: "Sunscreen = safed chehra?"
Hook 3: "Helmet pehenne se pehle ye ek galti mat karna." Visual: buckling the strap, stick raised to camera. Text: "Ye galti mat karna".
Hook 4: "[X] din, roz bike pe, sirf ye sunscreen." Visual: stick on the bike mirror, you swipe it mid-action. Text: "[X] din. Ek sunscreen." ([X] = days you really used it.)

PROBLEM (0:03-0:08)
Say it your way. Example: "Cream lagao toh chehra safed, helmet ke neeche chipchip. Isliye lagana hi chhod diya."
Show: squeeze an old tube (label hidden) into your palm, white streak on your cheek in the selfie cam.

DEMO AND PROOF (0:08-0:20)
Swipe the stick across forehead, cheeks and nose, blend, then show the same selfie angle in the same light.
Say exactly: "SPF 50, no white cast."
Say your way: how it feels, how long it took (time it on camera), the click of the cap. One detail you really noticed.

OBJECTION (0:20-0:25)
Doubt: "Rs 499 ek stick ke liye?" Only if true: "Tube ka kya fayda jo lagti hi nahi thi. Ye roz lagti hai, toh mere liye theek hai."
Optional, 2 s: [one real review from the brand's store page].

CTA AND DISCLOSURE (0:25-0:30)
Say: "Rs 499. Neeche Shop Now dabao." Text: "Shop Now: Rs 499". The Ad label is already on from 0:00.

SHOT AND TEXT LIST
1. Unboxing at the desk, cap click close-up.
2. Stick sliding out of the jacket pocket.
3. Close-up swipe on the cheek.
4. Helmet off at the gate.
5. Same angle, same light, before and after, only if real.
Text, in order: Ad | Paid partnership with [Brand]; hook text; Safed chehra. Chipchipa helmet.; SPF 50, no white cast; Rs 499; Shop Now.

samples.text: TITLE TAG: Balcony Vegetable Gardening in India: Complete Guide 2026 META DESCRIPTION: Grow vegetables on an apartment balcony in Pune, Bengaluru or Hyderabad: sunlight, pots, soil, season-wise crops, watering, pests and a 4-pot plan. # Balcony vegetable gardening in Indian cities: the complete guide Last updated: 7 October 2026 | By [writer name, one true credential, e.g. "grows on her own Pune balcony since [year]"] This guide is for first-time apartment gardeners in Pune, Bengaluru and Hyderabad. You have a balcony, a sunny ledge or a few square feet of terrace, and you want vegetables on the plate, not just green leaves. After reading it you can measure your sunlight, pick pots, mix soil and sow the right crops for the month. You can also water without drowning anything and set up a four-pot starter garden in one afternoon. [How we know: number of balconies tested, cities, dates, who tested them.] Where the advice depends on your city, we say so. ## Key takeaways - Count the hours of direct sun first. Leafy crops and herbs need about 3 to 4 hours, fruiting crops such as tomato, chilli and brinjal need 5 to 6 or more. - Every pot needs drainage holes. Depth matters more than width: 6 to 8 inches for greens, 12 inches or more for fruiting plants. - Do not fill pots with garden soil alone. Mix garden soil, cocopeat and vermicompost in equal parts. - Plant for the season, not the month you bought the pot. October to February suits methi, palak, dhania and cherry tomato in all three cities. - Water when the top two inches of soil are dry, in the morning. Most dying plants are overwatered, not underwatered. - Start with four pots. A small garden you tend daily beats a big one you abandon in week three. ## Table of contents 1. [How much sun does a balcony need for vegetables?](#sun) 2. [Which pots and containers work on a balcony?](#containers) 3. [What soil mix should you fill them with?](#soil) 4. [What can you grow in each season?](#seasons) 5. [How often should you water?](#watering) 6. [How do you handle pests without harsh chemicals?](#pests) 7. [What does a 4-pot starter balcony look like?](#example) 8. [Which mistakes and questions come up most?](#faqs) 9. [What should you do next?](#next) ## How much sun does a balcony need for vegetables? Leafy greens and herbs need roughly 3 to 4 hours of direct sun, while fruiting vegetables like tomato, chilli and brinjal need 5 to 6 hours or more. Direct means sunlight that actually lands on the leaves, not bright shade. Measure before you buy a single pot. On a normal day, check the same spot at 9 am, 12 noon and 3 pm. Note whether sun reaches it each time. Three "yes" answers means about six hours or more, which is a fruiting-crop spot. One or two means leafy crops and herbs. Direction helps as a first guess. South- and west-facing balconies get the longest sun in India. East-facing balconies get gentler morning sun, which is the easiest to grow in. North-facing balconies are the hardest, though the summer sun climbs high enough to give them some light. City matters too. In Hyderabad the afternoon sun on a west-facing balcony can scorch leaves in summer, so a green shade net across the top third of the railing is worth the small cost. Pune and Bengaluru balconies are kinder, but a west wall still bakes pots dry by evening. Measure in the season you plan to grow. A tower across the road can steal the winter sun just when you want tomatoes. Once you know your hours, you can choose containers that suit them. ## Which pots and containers work on a balcony? Pick any container with drainage holes and enough depth. Leafy greens need 6 to 8 inches, carrot about 12, and tomato, chilli and brinjal 12 to 18 inches (roughly 12 to 20 litres). Material comes second to depth and holes. | Container | Good for | Watch out for | |---|---|---| | Terracotta pot | Herbs, chilli, curry leaf | Heavy, dries fast in summer, cracks if dropped | | Plastic pot or bucket | Tomato, brinjal, mint | Holds water, so overwatering is easy; old plastic turns brittle in strong sun | | Fabric grow bag | Tomato, chilli, root vegetables | Dries fastest, so it needs daily checks in Hyderabad summers | | Long trough or crate | Methi, palak, dhania, lettuce | Needs holes drilled if it has none | | Railing planter | Herbs, leafy greens | Weight on the rail; ask your society office before you hang anything | A few practical points from small balconies: - Wet potting mix is heavy. Lift a full pot once before deciding how many to put on one side of the balcony. - Put a tray under every pot so water does not drip on the neighbour below. Empty the trays after rain, because standing water breeds mosquitoes. A big pot of poor soil still fails, so soil is the next decision. ## What soil mix should you fill them with? Use one part garden soil, one part cocopeat and one part vermicompost or well-rotted compost, plus a handful of neem cake per large pot. Garden soil alone packs hard in a pot, and cocopeat alone holds water but carries no food. Here is how to make it: 1. Soak a cocopeat block in water until it breaks apart. Squeeze it out, and rinse it once or twice if the product is not labelled "washed" or "low EC", because unwashed cocopeat can carry salts that stress seedlings. 2. Mix the cocopeat, garden soil and compost in a tub or on newspaper. It should feel crumbly, not sticky. 3. Add a handful of neem cake for each 15 to 20 litres of mix. It feeds slowly and puts off some soil pests. 4. Fill the pot to about two fingers below the rim, so water does not overflow. No garden soil on the 14th floor? Use two parts cocopeat to one part vermicompost, and plan to feed more often, since this mix is light and the food washes out faster. Feed fruiting plants with a diluted organic liquid feed (vermicompost tea or a ready liquid manure, used at the label's strength) every two weeks once they flower. Leafy greens can manage with the compost in the mix. With soil sorted, the question becomes what to put in it and when. ## What can you grow in each season? Grow winter crops from October to February, heat-tolerant crops from March to May and rain-friendly crops from June to September. Most first-time failures come from sowing a cool-season crop into summer heat, not from bad technique. | Season | Months | Grow | Skip or protect | |---|---|---|---| | Winter | October to February | Methi, palak, dhania, lettuce, radish, beetroot, carrot, cherry tomato, capsicum | Frost is not a worry in these cities, but cool nights slow chilli | | Summer | March to May | Okra (bhindi), amaranth (chaulai), cucumber on a trellis, chilli, brinjal, curry leaf | Move leafy greens to the shadiest corner or skip them; use shade net in Hyderabad | | Monsoon | June to September | Chilli, brinjal, okra, amaranth, basil, tulsi, ridge gourd on a trellis | Coriander and spinach rot in heavy rain; keep pots out of direct downpours in Pune | How the three cities differ: - **Pune:** cool winters suit leafy greens and tomatoes. Plan a covered corner for heavy monsoon rain. - **Bengaluru:** mild all year, so leafy crops last longer into summer. Cloudy July and August spells cut light for fruiting plants. - **Hyderabad:** winter is the sweet spot. Summer needs shade net, mulch and a daily watering check. For a first garden, choose crops that pay back quickly. Methi and dhania can be cut in about three to four weeks, mint grows from a cutting, and cherry tomato and chilli give fruit over many weeks once they start. Buy seedlings for tomato and chilli, and sow seed for methi, palak, dhania and radish. Sow seeds about two to three times as deep as the seed is wide. Choosing the crop is half the job. Keeping it alive is the other half, and that comes down to water. ## How often should you water? Water when the top two inches of soil feel dry, usually once a day in summer, every second day in winter and only when needed in the monsoon. Push a finger in to the second knuckle. Dry means water, damp means wait. The finger test beats any fixed schedule, because pots dry at different speeds. A terracotta pot on a west-facing balcony in Hyderabad may need water twice a day in May. A plastic pot in an east-facing Pune balcony in December may need it every third day. Some habits that help: - Water in the morning, at the soil, not over the leaves. Wet leaves at night invite fungus. - Water until it runs out of the bottom holes, then stop. Small sips every day keep roots shallow. - Cover the soil with a thin layer of dry leaves, coco husk or dried grass (mulch). It slows evaporation, which matters most from March to May. Even well-watered plants get visitors, so here is how to deal with pests. ## How do you handle pests without harsh chemicals? Check the underside of leaves twice a week, remove pests by hand or with a water jet, and spray neem oil in the evening if they return. Catching the first few aphids or whiteflies costs you two minutes. Catching a full infestation costs you the plant. Common balcony pests and what to do: | Pest | What you see | First response | |---|---|---| | Aphids | Clusters of tiny green or black insects on new shoots | Spray with a strong jet of water, wipe by hand, then neem | | Whitefly | White specks that fly up when you shake the plant | Yellow sticky traps near the plant, then neem | | Spider mites | Fine webbing and dull stippled leaves, worst in dry heat | Raise humidity, wash leaves, neem every few days | For a neem spray, follow the dilution on the bottle of your neem oil. Many labels suggest roughly 3 to 5 ml per litre of water with a few drops of mild liquid soap to help it mix. Spray in the evening, never in hot sun, and cover the underside of the leaves. Test on one leaf first and wait a day. Healthy plants resist pests better, so spacing and sun do more than any spray. Do not crowd pots against each other, and remove dead leaves from the soil. Now let us put everything together in a plan you can start this weekend. ## What does a 4-pot starter balcony look like? A workable first garden is four containers: one for a fruiting plant, one for chilli, one trough of leafy greens and one pot of mint. It fits in about a 2 by 4 foot corner and needs roughly ten minutes a day. The plan below is an illustrative set-up, not a case study. **The situation.** A 2BHK flat in Baner, Pune, with an east-facing balcony. The owner's 9 am, 12 noon and 3 pm check shows direct sun at 9 and 12 only, so about 4 hours of morning sun. It is the second week of October. That is enough for leafy crops and for tomato and chilli if they are placed in the brightest spot, though fruit may come a little slowly. **The four containers:** | Pot | Size | Planting | Position | |---|---|---|---| | A | 20 litre fabric bag, 14 inch deep | 1 cherry tomato seedling, with a stake or small cage | Brightest corner, at the rail end | | B | 12 litre pot | 1 chilli (hari mirch) seedling | Next to A, same light | | C | Trough about 24 x 8 inches, 8 inch deep | Methi, palak and dhania in three separate rows, about 4 inches apart | Middle, gets 3 to 4 hours | | D | 8 litre pot | 1 mint cutting, grown alone because it spreads | Shadiest corner | **The work.** Mix about 65 litres of soil in total (one part garden soil, one part cocopeat, one part vermicompost, neem cake in A and B). Fill, plant, water until it drains. Put trays under every pot. Stake the tomato on day one, not after it falls over. **The routine.** Water by the finger test each morning, which takes about five minutes. On Sundays, spend 20 minutes: check leaf undersides, nip off dead leaves, tie the tomato and give the liquid feed to A and B from the time they flower. **What to expect.** Methi and dhania are typically ready for a first cut in about 3 to 4 weeks, palak a little later. Cut the outer leaves and leave the centre to regrow. Cherry tomato and chilli take roughly 10 to 12 weeks from transplant to first fruit, so patience is part of the plan. These timings vary with sun, seedling age and weather, and none of this is a guaranteed harvest. [Our own result: photos, dates and weights from [Brand]'s test balcony, plus one thing that went wrong and what we changed. Add before publishing.] **Cost.** [Brand starter kit price and contents. Insert from the product page.] Plans meet questions, so here are the ones that come up most. ## Which mistakes and questions come up most? **Can I grow vegetables with only 3 hours of sun?** Yes, but choose leafy greens, mint and coriander. Tomato, chilli and brinjal will grow leaves and flower poorly in that light. Try dhania, palak, methi and lettuce first. **Why are the leaves turning yellow?** Soggy soil is the most common cause, especially in the monsoon. Check drainage holes and the saucer before you add any fertiliser. If the soil is fine and the older leaves are pale all over, the plant may need feeding. **Do I need to pollinate by hand?** Tomato and chilli flowers pollinate themselves, and a gentle tap on the stem or flower cluster in the morning helps. Cucumber and gourds have separate male and female flowers, so with few bees on a high floor you may need to move pollen with a soft brush. **What do I do when I travel?** Group the pots in light shade, water deeply before leaving, mulch the soil and ask someone to water once midway. Leafy greens suffer most, fruiting plants usually cope with a week. **Do I need permission from my society?** Pots on your own balcony floor rarely need it. Railing-hung planters, heavy troughs and anything that drips on a neighbour often do, so ask your society office first. Next, a step you can take today. ## What should you do next? Do your 9 am, 12 noon and 3 pm sun check this weekend, then pick your four pots. If you want everything in one box, the [Brand] Balcony Starter Kit ([contents and price]) comes with pots, cocopeat, vermicompost, neem cake and seeds sorted for your city and season. [Shop the starter kit](/shop/starter-kit) Keep reading: - [Terracotta vs plastic vs fabric pots: which suits your balcony](/guides/pots) - [Cocopeat vs garden soil: how to mix potting soil for containers](/guides/potting-mix) - [Month-by-month sowing calendar for Pune, Bengaluru and Hyderabad](/guides/sowing-calendar) - [How to make a neem oil spray for balcony plants](/guides/neem-spray) - [Vegetables that grow in low light: a shade balcony list](/guides/low-light-vegetables)

[BRAND] WI-FI SMART PLUG, MODEL [MODEL]: USER GUIDE

About this guide
This guide is for first-time smart-home users. It covers the [Brand] Wi-Fi Smart Plug (the plug). You need a smartphone and a home Wi-Fi router. Text in **bold** is a button or label exactly as shown on the plug or in the app. Note means useful extra information. Caution means risk of damage. Warning means risk of injury or fire.

Safety information
Warning: Use the plug only in a dry, indoor place. Never touch it with wet hands.
Warning: Do not connect an appliance above [SPEC: rated load in watts and amps]. Check the wattage printed on the appliance label first.
Warning: Do not cover the plug while an appliance is connected.
[STATUTORY: BIS registration and marking line, from the compliance owner]
[STATUTORY: e-waste disposal line, from the compliance owner]

What is in the box
- 1 [Brand] Wi-Fi Smart Plug
- 1 quick start card
- 1 warranty card
[Confirm against the packing list.]

Before you start
- A phone running [SPEC: minimum Android and iOS versions].
- Your home Wi-Fi name and password. The plug supports [SPEC: Wi-Fi band].
- A working internet connection.

Quick start
1. Push the plug into a wall socket. The indicator light blinks [SPEC: colour and speed].
2. On your phone, install the **[Brand] Home** app from Google Play or the App Store. The app icon appears on your phone.
3. Create your account in the app with your mobile number. An OTP arrives by SMS. After you enter it, the **Home** screen opens.
4. Tap **Add Device**. The app shows a list of device types.
5. Choose **Smart Plug**. The app asks for your Wi-Fi name and password.
6. Enter your Wi-Fi password. The **Connect** button turns active.
7. Tap **Connect**. Wait up to [SPEC: seconds]. The indicator light stops blinking and the app shows the plug on the **Home** screen.

Note: If step 7 fails, go to Troubleshooting.

Schedule the geyser to switch off
Warning: Before step 1, read the wattage on your geyser's label. If it is above [SPEC: rated load], do not use this plug with the geyser.
Warning: Use a dry socket that stays out of water splashes. If your geyser socket is in a wet area, ask an electrician first.
1. Push the geyser's cable into the plug. Nothing switches on yet.
2. Keep the geyser's own switch in the ON position. The plug now controls its power.
3. Open the app and tap the plug on the **Home** screen. The plug's control screen opens.
4. Tap the name at the top and change it to **Geyser**. The **Home** screen now shows **Geyser**.
5. Tap **Schedule**. The schedule list opens. It is empty.
6. Tap **Add Schedule**. A setup screen opens.
7. Set **Time** to when the geyser must switch off, for example 7:00 AM. The time shows on the screen.
8. Set **Action** to **Off**. The screen shows **Off**.
9. Under **Repeat**, tap each day you want. Chosen days turn highlighted.
10. Tap **Save**. The schedule appears in the list with its switch turned on.
11. Test it. Set a schedule for two minutes from now, then wait. At that time the app shows **Geyser** as **Off**.

Note: This chapter covers switching off only. For switching on by schedule, follow [SAFETY REF: brand guidance].
Note: The schedule uses your phone's time. Check that it shows Indian Standard Time.

Troubleshooting
| Problem | Likely cause | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Indicator light does not blink | Socket has no power, or the plug is loose | Test the socket with a lamp. Push the plug in fully. |
| App cannot find the plug | Phone is on mobile data, or far from the router | Turn on phone Wi-Fi and turn off mobile data. Stand within [SPEC: range] of the router. |
| Connection fails after step 7 | Wrong Wi-Fi password, or an unsupported band | Re-enter the password. Passwords are case-sensitive. If your router uses one name for two bands, see [SUPPORT ARTICLE]. |
| OTP does not arrive | Weak signal or a blocked sender | Wait 2 minutes. Check network signal. Tap **Resend OTP**. |
| App shows the plug as **Offline** | Router off, power cut or no internet | Restore power and internet. Reopen the app. |
| Geyser does not switch off at the set time | Schedule switch is off, a day is not selected, or phone time is wrong | Open **Schedule**. Turn the switch on, tick the day and check the phone time. |
| Plug switches off by itself | The load may be above the rating | Unplug the geyser. Check its wattage against [SPEC: rated load]. |
| Plug is hot or smells burnt | Overload or a fault | Unplug it at once. Stop using it. Call support. |

Specifications, care and support

FLYOVER JAM: "Why every new flyover in Indian cities makes traffic worse"
Narration: Roman Hinglish. Part 1 of the essay: cold open, thesis, context and chapter 1.

COLD OPEN
[CLIP: local news inauguration of a flyover in any Indian city, 0:05-0:15, credit the channel by name. Why: it shows the official promise, the empty road.]
Teen saal pehle ek flyover ka udghatan hua. Neta ji ne ribbon kaata, aur camera ne wahi shot liya jo har flyover ka hota hai: khaali sadak, tez chalti gaadiyan.
[GRAPHIC: date stamp "Day 1"]
Us din sach mein jam nahi tha.
Ab wahin khade ho jaiye. Shaam ke chhe baje. Flyover ke upar jam. Flyover ke neeche jam. Aur beech mein aap, ek hi signal par teesri baar hari batti miss karte hue.
[CLIP: drone shot of the same kind of flyover at evening peak, credit the creator. Why: the contrast with Day 1.]
Sawaal seedha hai. Agar flyover jam hatane ke liye banta hai, to jam wapas kaise aa gaya?
Aur jawab flyover ki galti nahi hai. Jawab uska gannit hai.

THESIS, STAKES AND ROADMAP
Meri baat ek line mein: naya flyover traffic kam nahi karta. Wo safar ko aasaan banata hai, aur jab safar aasaan hota hai, to zyada log zyada safar karte hain, jab tak jam wapas wahin nahi pahunch jaata.
Ye sirf aapke waqt ka maamla nahi hai. Ek flyover karodon ka kharcha hota hai. [SOURCE NEEDED: cost of one recent flyover in an Indian city] To sawaal ye bhi hai ki wo paisa kahin aur lagta, to kya hota?
Aur saaf kar dun: main ye nahi keh raha ki flyover kabhi nahi banna chahiye. Main ye keh raha hoon ki "jam hatane ke liye" flyover banana alag baat hai.
Is video mein chaar cheezein dekhenge. Ek, sasti sadak aur zyada gaadiyan. Do, jam jaata nahi, bas khisakta hai. Teen, flyover gaadi ginta hai, insaan nahi. Chaar, kya flyover kabhi kaam bhi karta hai? Is hisse mein hum pehli cheez tak jaayenge.

CONTEXT
Pehle flyover banane wale ko bewakoof mat samajhiye. Unka logic saaf hai. Signal par gaadiyan ruk-ruk kar line banati hain. Signal hata do, line hat jaayegi.
Aur shuru mein ye sach bhi hota hai. Pehle kuch mahine sadak sach mein khuli rehti hai. Dikkat ye hai ki hum us pehle hisse ko poori kahani maan lete hain.
Aur ek baat aur. Planner kehte hain ki hamare sheharon mein gaadiyan har saal badh rahi hain, isliye sadak chaudi karni hi padegi. Ye is bahes ka sabse mazboot jawab hai, aur hum use poori izzat ke saath sunenge, chapter chaar mein.
Tab tak ek kaam kijiye. Ek flyover dimaag mein rakhiye, jise aap roz paar karte hain. Video ke end mein hum usi par argument ko test karenge.
Aapke WhatsApp group mein bhi yahi line chalti hai: ek aur flyover bana do, sab theek ho jaayega. Aaj dekhte hain, sach mein?

CHAPTER 1: SASTI SADAK, ZYADA GAADIYAN
Ek experiment karte hain. Maan lo aap roz Charbagh se Gomti Nagar jaate ho. Ek naya flyover banta hai, aur aapka safar pehle se kaafi chhota ho jaata hai.
[GRAPHIC: label "Maan lo", clearly a made-up example, not data]
Ab dekhiye ki sirf aapka nahi, aur logon ka faisla bhi badalta hai. Chaar tarah ke log.
Pehle, jo jam se bachne ke liye subah jaldi nikalte the. Ab sadak khaali dikh rahi hai, to wo bhi aath baje ke aas-paas nikalne lagte hain. Wahi sadak, wahi peak.
Doosre, jo bus ya metro se jaate the. Flyover par gaadi ka safar tez dikhta hai, to bike ya car ka sauda sasta lagne lagta hai.
Teesre, jo safar tha hi nahi. Weekend par Gomti Nagar ke mall ka plan, jo jam ke darr se hamesha taal dete the. Ab chale jaate hain. Ye naya traffic hai. Pehle isse sadak par ginti hi nahi thi.
Chauthe, aur ye sabse dheere hota hai. Jahan flyover pahunchata hai, wahan zameen bikti hai. Log door ghar lete hain, kyunki ab door rehna sehan ho jaata hai. Aur door ka matlab hai har din lamba safar.
[GRAPHIC: four icons appearing one by one: clock, bus, mall, house]
Yaad rakhiye, in chaaron mein se koi galat kaam nahi kar raha. Har insaan apne liye sahi faisla le raha hai. Problem ye hai ki sabke sahi faisle mil kar sadak ko wapas bhar dete hain.
Isiliye udghatan wali tasveer jhooth nahi bolti. Wo bas jaldi bolti hai. Wo us din ki tasveer hai, jab faislon ko badalne ka waqt hi nahi mila tha.
Ye sirf andaza nahi hai. Do economists, Gilles Duranton aur Matthew Turner, ne America ke sheharon ka data dekha. Unhone paaya ki jaise-jaise sheher mein sadkein badhi, gaadiyon ka chalna lagbhag utna hi badha.
[SOURCE: Duranton and Turner, "The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion", American Economic Review, 2011. Confirm the wording of the finding before recording.]
Isi ko kehte hain induced demand. Matlab, sadak ne maang paida ki.
Ab aap kahoge ki gaadiyan to aabadi badhne se bhi badhti hain. Bilkul. Induced demand ka matlab ye nahi ki flyover akela gaadiyan paida karta hai. Matlab ye hai ki wo badhotri ko jaldi sadak par le aata hai, aur flyover ka faayda usi mein kho jaata hai.
Sawaal fair hai: ye America ka data hai, India mein bhi aisa hota hai? Sach ye hai ki hamare sheharon par saaf, bharosemand data kam hai. [SOURCE NEEDED: a study of travel time before and after a flyover in an Indian city] Lekin tarika wahi hai, aur aap ise apni gali mein dekh sakte ho.
Sadak par hum paise se nahi, waqt se bhugtan karte hain. Flyover waqt ka daam ghata deta hai. Aur jab daam girta hai, to maang badhti hai. Bilkul jaise free delivery. Delivery free ho jaaye to aap zyada order karte ho, chahe zaroorat utni na ho. Ya ghar ka example lijiye. Jis din naya fridge aata hai, aap zyada saaman bharte ho. Jagah badhi, to saaman badha.
[GRAPHIC: a simple price-and-demand drawing, "Cost of a trip = time", with the line sliding down]
Isliye jam kam hone ki ek hadd hoti hai. Log tab tak aate rehte hain jab tak safar phir utna thakaane wala na ho jaaye jitna pehle tha. Jam ek tarah ka level hai. Aap use neeche dabate ho, aur wo wapas upar aa jaata hai.
Ab aap kahoge: theek hai bhai, itni gaadiyan aa gayi, to flyover ke upar to bhaagti honi chahiye. Jam neeche hona chahiye, ya wahan jahan flyover khatam hota hai.
Aap sahi pakad rahe ho. Wahin se agla chapter shuru hota hai. Flyover jam hatata nahi. Wo jam ko ek jagah se uthakar doosri jagah rakh deta hai. Aur jahan flyover utarta hai, ek tang sadak aapka intezaar kar rahi hai.
[CLIP: drone footage of a flyover exit merging into a narrow road at peak hour, credit the creator. Why: it previews chapter 2.]

TITLE OPTIONS (YouTube)
1. Flyover banao, jam badhao? Naye flyover ke baad traffic kyun nahi ghatta
2. Har naya flyover jam badhata hai? Induced demand ki sachchai (Hinglish)

01:50 Flyover kyun bante hain

06:30 Agla chapter: jam khisakta hai

DESCRIPTION SOURCES
Duranton and Turner, "The Fundamental Law of Road Congestion", American Economic Review, 2011: [link]. [Add the Indian-city study and flyover cost sources here.]

VSL SCRIPT: [Brand] Client Voice, 8-week spoken-English programme for IT support staff
Format: text on screen with English voice-over, one line per slide, about 13 minutes. Hinglish lines are said and shown as written. Button under the video: "Enrol now".

[HOOK 0:00-0:50]
You fix tickets faster than anyone on your shift.
Then a client joins the call, and you go quiet.
Not because you don't know the answer.
You know it. It's right there.
But the sentence won't come out the way it sounds in your head.
Aap jaante ho dikkat kya hai. Bas bolte waqt line nahi milti.
If that's you, stay for the next few minutes.
This is for IT support staff, aged 24 to 32, who've been told: "Next step is client-facing."
And who felt their stomach drop when they heard it.
I'll show you why that happens.
It has nothing to do with how smart you are.
Then I'll show you the 8-week programme we built to fix it.
The price, the refund and everything included, said plainly before the end.
Watch till then, and decide for yourself.

[PROBLEM AND AGITATION 0:50-3:30]
Let's take a normal Tuesday.
A client's dashboard goes down.
You find the cause. You fix it. The ticket is closed.
Then the client's manager joins the call.
"Can someone explain what happened?"
Your senior looks at you.
Your heart speeds up.
You know exactly what happened.
Out comes: "Sir, actually, the server, it was, like, down, so we..."
You hear yourself. You stop.
The line goes quiet for two seconds. It feels like two minutes.
You say, "I'll send a mail."
Then you spend an hour writing one perfect email.
It reads beautifully.
That's the strange part.
For most people on a support desk, written English is fine.
Reading logs, writing tickets, replying to mails, all fine.
The trouble is live English.
No time to edit. No backspace.
And nobody ever trained you for that part.
So here's what it quietly costs you.
Your senior's name is on the client call. Yours isn't.
The credit for your fix goes to whoever spoke.
Your manager says, "Client-facing roles need good communication."
You nod. And you hear: "Not you."
Meanwhile someone who knows half of what you know gets the client account.
Ye unfair lagta hai. Aur hai bhi.
You start avoiding calls.
You let others unmute first.
On Monday's stand-up, you rehearse one line in your head.
Then they ask a different question, and the line is useless.
Samajh sab aata hai. Bolna nahi aata.
So you say, "Yes, working on it." And you hope that's enough.
You tell yourself, "I'm just not a talker."
Then a year goes by.
Same desk. Same shift. Same tickets.
And the thought stays: "Will I ever move up from here?"
If you've had that thought, you're not lazy.
You're not "weak in English."
You've just never been taught the one skill this job asks for.
Let me show you what that skill actually is.

[STORY AND DISCOVERY 3:30-5:30]
I'm [founder name], and I run [Brand] in Hyderabad.
[One true sentence on the founder's background: role, years, company type. Insert only facts you can show.]
[One true sentence on the moment a client call went wrong for you or for a student you worked with. Use real details, with consent.]
I did what everyone does first.
I tried to fix my English.

samples.text:
MEETHA HISAAB

Episode 1: "Pehli Kadhai"

Written by [Writer name]
Draft 1, 7 October 2026
[Contact: email, phone]

COLD OPEN

INT. GOPAL MISHTHAN BHANDAR, RAJWADA, INDORE - DAWN

Black. A steel shutter RATTLES. It sticks halfway. A hammer BANGS it free and light spills in.

Dust hangs over a glass counter. One tray of balushahi sits there, hard as river stones. Above the counter hangs a garlanded photo of GOPAL PRASAD SHARMA (60s), laughing.

Three silhouettes duck under the shutter. ANJALI (34, crisp salwar, laptop bag, a phone she holds like a secret), ROHAN (30, kurta on inside-out, holding the hammer), and TANMAY (24, a ring light on a stand, already filming).

TANMAY
(to phone)
Day one, guys. Gopal Mishthan Bhandar, since 1974. We're back.

ANJALI
Who are you talking to?

TANMAY
Four hundred and twelve followers.

ANJALI
Switch it off.

TANMAY
It's live.

Anjali looks at the photo. Rohan puts the hammer on the counter, very gently, as if it might wake someone.

At the back, a wide black kadhai sits on a cold coal stove. Next to it, a school notebook with a rubber band around it. On the cover, in a father's blue ink: JALEBI. DO NOT TOUCH.

Rohan touches it. He reads aloud, in his best filmy voice.

ROHAN
"Chaasni ki taar... jab tak aankh na bole."

ANJALI
What does that mean?

ROHAN
It means Papa has beaten us. Even from the photo.

Tanmay sets the ring light on the stove. Rohan lights the coal. Anjali holds the notebook open like an exam paper. They pour batter into the kadhai.

It does not become a jalebi. It becomes a brown map of Madhya Pradesh.

SHARMA JI (60s, the shop next door, towel on his shoulder) appears at the shutter with a bucket.

SHARMA JI
Aag lagi hai?

ROHAN
Nahi, Sharma ji. Jalebi.

Smoke rolls out of the shop. Sharma ji throws the bucket. Water hits the kadhai, the coal, the ring light, and Tanmay's phone. A long hiss.

TANMAY
(to a dead phone)
Four hundred and twelve followers... are now watching the ceiling.

Anjali opens the notebook's last page. In the same blue ink, one line.

ANJALI
(reading)
"Diwali tak chalana. Phir dekhna."

She looks up at the photo. The photo goes on laughing.

SMASH CUT TO TITLE: MEETHA HISAAB. Under it: DIWALI MEIN 42 DIN.

ACT ONE

INT. GOPAL MISHTHAN BHANDAR - MORNING

The smoke has thinned. The three siblings sit on plastic stools in a row, smelling of burnt sugar. VAKIL TRIVEDI (50s, safari suit, a brown envelope in a plastic cover) stands at the counter. With him is JAGDISH CHACHA (50s, gold chain, a smile with too many teeth), Papa's younger brother.

VAKIL TRIVEDI
Your father left one condition. He asked me to read it only after the terahvi.

ROHAN
It's been three days since the terahvi.

VAKIL TRIVEDI
I am a careful man.

He opens the envelope.

VAKIL TRIVEDI (CONT'D)
"Mere teeno bachche Diwali ki raat tak dukaan chalayenge. Us raat ki bahi mein ghata nahi hona chahiye. Ek rupaya bhi zyada chalega." If that is done, the shop and the flat upstairs are yours. All three.

TANMAY
One rupee?

VAKIL TRIVEDI
His words.

JAGDISH CHACHA
(stepping in, warm)
And if the books say otherwise, the shop comes to me. I'll sell it. Builder friend of mine, very good man, three floors, glass front.

ANJALI
You've already spoken to a builder.

JAGDISH CHACHA
I plan ahead. Like your father. (beat) Almost like.

He pats the counter and leaves. A bell over the door TINKLES for him, the only cheerful thing in the room.

INT. SHOP, BACK OFFICE - DAY

A cubicle behind the counter. A steel almirah, a calendar from 2019, a wall of invoices. Anjali sits with a thick ledger. She flips the pages with a pencil. The pencil stays in the red.

On the desk, her phone lights up. A preview, partly visible: "OFFER LETTER: SENIOR ANALYST, PUNE. Reply by Friday."

She turns the phone face down. Rohan swings in with a tray.

ROHAN
Gold-leaf gulab jamun. Rs 80 a piece. Rich people only.

ANJALI
What did it cost?

ROHAN
Cost is a negative way of looking at it.

ANJALI
We owe the khoya supplier a lot of money, Rohan. Not "a lot". A number with four commas in it.

ROHAN
Indian commas or American commas?

She does not laugh. Tanmay enters, ring light under one arm.

TANMAY
Content plan. Day in the life of a mithai shop. Behind the kadhai. "Jalebi fails," that's a series.

ANJALI
We are not filming our failures.

TANMAY
People love failures. It's called authenticity.

BHURA KAKA (60s, the old karigar, a cloth bag on his shoulder) stands in the doorway. Nobody heard him arrive.

BHURA KAKA
Kai chalo, bacchon. Ghano garam hai, pehle chaas piyo.

He puts down three small glasses of buttermilk. Then, quietly:

BHURA KAKA (CONT'D)
Main kal se nahi aaunga.

ROHAN
Kaka?

BHURA KAKA
Ikatalis saal. Gopal bhaiya ke saath. Ab unke bina kadhai ke saamne khada hota hoon, haath kaampte hain.

ANJALI
We can't do this without you.

BHURA KAKA
Mere saath bhi nahi kar sakte. Mujhe aadhi recipes aati hain. Baaki aadhi unke dimaag mein thi. Aur us copy mein.

Anjali opens the notebook. She flips. A long pause.

ANJALI
There are pages missing.

She holds it up. A neat torn edge runs down the spine. Four pages gone.

INT. STAIRWELL, BETWEEN SHOP AND FLAT - LATE AFTERNOON

Narrow concrete stairs, a bicycle chained to the railing. Anjali sits on the third step, phone at her ear, voice low.

RITU (V.O.)
Anjali, the team is very keen. Joining is the first of November. Diwali week or not, I need your answer by Friday.

ANJALI
My father passed away last month, Ritu. The shop needs me.

RITU (V.O.)
I understand. I can hold it till Friday. Not longer.

A shoe SCUFFS above. Tanmay is leaning over the railing, headphones around his neck.

TANMAY
Pune?

ANJALI
(into phone, brightly)
Yes, the poha supplier. Pune ka poha. I'll call back.

She ends the call. Tanmay stares.

TANMAY
Didi. Pune ka poha? In Indore? That's treason.

ANJALI
It's a joke. Go and mop the floor.

He goes, not convinced. She sits there a moment longer, the phone warm in her hand.

INT. SHOP - AFTERNOON

The shop is open, and empty. A ceiling fan turns. The siblings stand behind the counter like three bad salesmen. Rohan arranges balushahi in a pyramid. It collapses.

A black landline phone on the counter RINGS. All three stare at it. Nobody has called that phone in years.

Anjali lifts it.

ANJALI
Gopal Mishthan Bhandar.

INTERCUT: INT. KHANNA AUTO COMPONENTS, OFFICE - DAY

MR. KHANNA (50s, a calculator on his desk, a Diwali list in front of him) speaks into a speakerphone.

MR. KHANNA
Gopal ji ki dukaan? Main Khanna bol raha hoon. Har Diwali Gopal ji soan papdi bhejte the. Poore Indore mein sabse badhiya. Woh...

ANJALI
Papa ka pichhle mahine dehant ho gaya, Khanna ji. Main unki beti bol rahi hoon.

MR. KHANNA
(a long breath)
Maaf karna, beta. Mujhe pata nahi tha. Dukaan khuli hai na?

ANJALI
Khuli hai.

MR. KHANNA
Achha. Kyunki mujhe teen sau dibbe chahiye. Staff aur dealers ke liye. Soan papdi aur kaju katli, gold box mein, hamare logo ke saath. Dhanteras se do din pehle tak.

Anjali covers the mouthpiece. Her eyes are on the ledger's red.

ANJALI
(whispering)
Teen sau dibbe.

ROHAN
(whispering)
Kitne ka?

ANJALI
(whispering)
Itna ki bahi ek rupaya aage nikal jaaye.

MR. KHANNA
Beta, line par ho?

Rohan mouths "YES". Tanmay mouths "CONTENT". Bhura Kaka, in the doorway, shakes his head slowly, no.

INT. SHOP - EVENING

The lights are half off. The siblings and Bhura Kaka stand around the notebook on the counter. The landline's long wire stretches across the counter like a leash.

ANJALI
Soan papdi un phate hue panno mein thi. Hai na, Kaka?

BHURA KAKA
Haan.

ROHAN
Toh nahi. Hum mana kar dete hain.

ANJALI
Mana karenge, toh bahi laal rahegi. Aur Jagdish Chacha ko apna glass front mil jaayega.

TANMAY
Hum haan bol sakte hain. Aur fail ho sakte hain.

ANJALI
Chupke se fail hona aur zor se fail hona, ek jaisa nahi hota.

She looks at her phone, still face down. She turns it over. The preview still reads: Reply by Friday.

She picks up the landline again. She doesn't speak. Mr. Khanna is still on hold, a thin classical tune humming from the receiver.

BHURA KAKA
(softly)
Bitiya. Teen sau dibbe. Teen aadmi. Ek kadhai. Aur ek kaagaz jo hai hi nahi.

ANJALI
Toh hum kaagaz dhoondh lenge.

She puts the receiver to her ear.

ANJALI (CONT'D)
Khanna ji. Teen sau dibbe, Dhanteras se do din pehle. Ho jaayega.

Rohan lets out a cheer. Tanmay films it, which is no longer allowed, but she lets it go.

With her other hand, thumb shaking, Anjali opens her phone. A reply box. She types two words to Pune: "I accept." She looks at them. She sends.

The swoosh of the sent message. She turns the phone face down once more.

ROHAN
(delighted)
Anjali di. Aapne abhi Papa ko jeet liya.

ANJALI
(not turning)
Aisa mat bolo. Abhi nahi.

Above the counter, the photo. For the first time, it is not laughing. It is just looking at her.

SUPER: DIWALI MEIN 41 DIN

samples.text:
WEBINAR SCRIPT: "Writing appraisal feedback that does not demotivate"
45 minutes, English, for HR managers at companies of 50 to 500 people in India. Host: [Speaker name], [title], [Brand] (HR-tech, Pune). Moderator: [Moderator name]. Cues in capitals are not spoken.

OUTCOME
By the end, every attendee will have rewritten one real feedback note so that the person receiving it knows exactly what to keep doing or change.

RUN OF SHOW
0:00-0:03 Pre-roll and housekeeping, Poll 1
0:03-0:06 Promise and agenda
0:06-0:17 Block 1: Describe what you saw, not who they are (written out below)
0:17-0:26 Block 2: Add the impact and one clear ask
0:26-0:34 Block 3: Test the note before it goes out
0:34-0:42 Live Q&A
0:42-0:44 Recap: three actions
0:44-0:45 Next step: the feedback template

PRE-ROLL AND HOUSEKEEPING (0:00-0:03)
SLIDE: "Welcome. Questions go in chat, any time."
MODERATOR: Good afternoon, everyone. Thanks for joining. I'm [Moderator name]. Type your name and company size in the chat as you come in.
MODERATOR: Two housekeeping points. Ask questions in the chat whenever you like, and we'll take them in the last eight minutes. And yes, you'll get the recording and the template by email afterwards. [Confirm.]
POLL 1 (launch now): "What is the hardest part of writing appraisal feedback? A. Finding the right words. B. Finding the time. C. Fear of how the person will react. D. Remembering what actually happened."
MODERATOR: Take a few seconds and vote. We'll look at the result in a minute.

PROMISE AND AGENDA (0:03-0:06)
SLIDE: "Today you will rewrite one feedback note."
HOST: Thanks, [Moderator name]. Let me look at the poll. [Read the result aloud and comment on the top two answers.]
HOST: Here's what we'll do today. By the end of this session, you will have rewritten one real feedback note. It can be one you wrote or one you have to review. The person reading it should know exactly what to keep doing or change.
HOST: This is the agenda. First, how to describe what you saw instead of who the person is. Second, how to add the impact and one clear ask. Third, a simple test to run before the note goes out. Then questions, then a short recap.
HOST: Quick intro. I'm [Speaker name]. [One true line on your HR or people-ops background.] At [Brand], we build appraisal software, and [one true line on what you have seen in real appraisal notes].
SLIDE: "Agenda: 1. What you saw. 2. Impact and ask. 3. The test."

BLOCK 1: DESCRIBE WHAT YOU SAW, NOT WHO THEY ARE (0:06-0:17)
SLIDE: "Labels vs behaviour"
SLIDE bullets: "A label is a conclusion." / "A behaviour is what a camera records."

HOST: Let's start with the single most common reason appraisal feedback demotivates people. It's not harshness. It's labels.
HOST: You know the words. "Lacks ownership." "Needs to be more proactive." "Attitude issue." "Not a team player." "Communication needs improvement."
HOST: I'd bet that every one of you has written at least one of these, or approved one this year. I have, too.
HOST: Here's the problem. A label is a conclusion. The manager looked at a month of small moments, drew a conclusion, and wrote only the conclusion down.
HOST: Now think about the person reading it. They see "lacks ownership." What do they do with that? They can't act on it. They don't know which moment you mean. All they can do is feel judged.
HOST: And when a person feels judged and can't act, they do one of two things. They argue, or they go quiet. Neither helps you.
HOST: So the first rule is this. Replace the label with behaviour.
SLIDE: "Behaviour = what a camera would record"
HOST: Here's the test. Could a camera have recorded it? A camera can record "Rohit sent the proposal with last quarter's numbers." A camera cannot record "Rohit is careless."
HOST: Let me show you with an example from a company that looks like yours. Say, a 150-person firm in Pune, a services company. A sales executive, Rohit. The manager's note says: "Rohit lacks attention to detail."
SLIDE: "Before: 'Rohit lacks attention to detail.'"
HOST: Read it from Rohit's side. Which detail? When? Is this about one proposal or everything he's done in a year? He has no way to know.
HOST: Now let's rewrite it. We start with the situation, which is when and where. Then the behaviour, which is what he did, in plain words.
SLIDE: "After: 'In the client review on the 12th, the proposal went out with last quarter's pricing.'"
HOST: That's a sentence about one moment. There's no insult in it. Rohit can recognise it, remember it, and, if he disagrees, tell you what he saw. That conversation is possible. The first one isn't.
HOST: Let me give you two more, quickly.
HOST: The label: "Kavita is not a team player."
SLIDE: "Before: 'Kavita is not a team player.'"
HOST: Ask yourself: what did Kavita do, or not do? Maybe at the Friday sync she kept the month-end numbers to herself and the team never saw them. Say that.
SLIDE: "After: 'At the Friday sync, the month-end figures were not shared with the accounts team until the following Monday.'"
HOST: Notice what we didn't write. We didn't say why. We didn't guess her intention. Maybe she was waiting for approval. Maybe she was overloaded. You don't know. So you describe, and you ask later.
HOST: One more.
SLIDE: "Before: 'Needs to be more proactive.'"
HOST: This is the most loved label in Indian appraisals. Proactive about what?
SLIDE: "After: 'The vendor payment delay in July was raised by the vendor, not by you. I'd like to hear about delays before the vendor calls.'"
HOST: Now, I did sneak in something extra there. The last sentence is a request. That's block two. For now, just look at the first sentence. It describes a thing that happened.
SLIDE: "Camera test: who, when, what they did or said"
HOST: So here is your camera test. Three questions. Who? When? What did they do or say? If your sentence answers all three, it's behaviour. If it has words like "attitude," "careless," "proactive," or "lazy," it's a label.
HOST: There are two traps that look like behaviour but aren't.
SLIDE: "Trap 1: always and never. Trap 2: mind-reading."
HOST: Trap one: "always" and "never." "Arjun is always late." Always? Nobody counted. It's a label wearing a number's clothes. Write what the calendar shows: "Arjun joined three of this month's morning stand-ups after the first five minutes."
HOST: Trap two is mind-reading. "Meera doesn't care about deadlines." You can't see caring. You can see that the report was due on Thursday and arrived on Monday. Write that, and then ask Meera what happened.
HOST: Both traps feel like facts, because we believe our own conclusions. The camera test catches both.
HOST: And a warning for those of you who review other people's notes. HR often gets the manager's draft the night before the cycle closes. You don't have to rewrite it. Just ask the manager one question: "What did you actually see?" That one question fixes a lot of notes.
HOST: Let's check in. Open the chat.
CHAT CHECK-IN: "Type one label you've written or approved in the last cycle. Just the label. No names."
MODERATOR: [Read five or six labels aloud as they arrive. Thank people for being honest.]
HOST: Thank you. See, we all have a few. It's not a failure. It's a habit, and a habit can change.

SLIDE: "Your turn: 4 minutes"
HOST: Now your turn, and this is the most important four minutes of today.
HOST: Take one feedback note. It can be one you wrote, one you're about to write, or one a manager sent you. Pick one sentence from it that is a label.
HOST: Write down the answers to three questions. Who? When? What did they do or say? Then write one sentence from those answers. Only one sentence. Don't fix the rest.
HOST: Use a notepad, a doc, whatever's in front of you. I'll be quiet for four minutes. Then I'll ask a few of you to paste your sentence in the chat.
[SILENT TIMER: 4 minutes. Show the slide with the three questions.]
HOST: Time. Some of you are still writing, and that's fine. Don't send the whole thing. Paste only the one sentence in the chat. Remove the name if it's a real person.
MODERATOR: [Read three or four rewritten sentences aloud. The host comments briefly on each: "That's camera-ready," or "Which meeting was that? Add the date."]
HOST: Look at what just happened. Four minutes ago, you had a label. Now you have a sentence a person can actually recognise.
HOST: But a recognisable sentence is only half a note. The person still asks, "So what?" That brings us to block two.
SLIDE: "Next: impact and ask"

BLOCK 2: ADD THE IMPACT AND ONE CLEAR ASK (0:17-0:26)
SLIDE bullets: "Impact: what it caused" / "Ask: one thing, next cycle" / "Keep the good: say what to repeat"
HOST: A behaviour sentence tells the person what happened. The impact tells them why you're writing it down. Let's go back to Rohit.
NOTES: Take the Rohit sentence and add the impact ("The client asked for a re-send, which cost the account team a day"). Then add one ask ("Before sending, check pricing against the master sheet"). Show a good-news example too. Strengths need behaviour as well ("Priya's handover notes in the August audit let a new joiner finish the file alone"). Warn: one ask per note; three asks becomes a list of faults.
HOST: And please don't skip the good news. Strengths need the same treatment: who, when, what they did. "Great team player" is as useless to Priya as "careless" is to Rohit.
POLL 2 (launch at the end of this block): "Which note would you rather receive? A. 'Needs to be more proactive.' B. 'The vendor delay in July came to light when the vendor called. I'd like to hear about delays before they do.'"
NOTES: Read the result. B should win. Ask anyone who voted A: "What would you have to know to act on A?"

BLOCK 3: TEST THE NOTE BEFORE IT GOES OUT (0:26-0:34)
SLIDE bullets: "Read-back test" / "Tone check" / "Rating and note must agree"
NOTES: Read-back test: read the note aloud as the person receiving it. Could they name the moment you mean? Tone check: remove adverbs and intensifiers ("always", "never", "completely"). Rating and note must agree: a high rating with a note full of faults, or the reverse, tells the person you didn't mean either. HOST: Before a note goes out, read it aloud as the person receiving it. If they can't name the moment you mean, it isn't ready.
Offer the 5-minute template check from the downloadable file. CHAT CHECK-IN: "Type 'yes' if your rewritten sentence passes the read-back test."

LIVE Q&A (0:34-0:42)
MODERATOR LINES: "We have a few minutes for questions. Type them in the chat. I'll read them out."
SEEDED QUESTIONS (use only if the chat is quiet):
1. What if a manager refuses to change a label?
2. How do I give behaviour feedback when the problem is attitude in a client meeting?
3. How long should a good feedback note be?
4. Should the same note go to the employee and to HR records?
5. What if the employee disagrees with the facts?
OFF-TOPIC: "Good question, and it needs more time than we have. Let me take it by email after the session."

RECAP: THREE ACTIONS (0:42-0:44)
SLIDE: "Three actions"
HOST: Three things to do this week. One, find one label in a pending note and replace it with who, when and what they did or said. Two, add the impact and one ask. Three, read the note aloud as the person receiving it before it goes out.

NEXT STEP (0:44-0:45)
SLIDE: "Download the feedback template: [link]"
HOST: If you'd like a one-page template with the camera test and the three questions, the link is on screen and in the chat. It's free. [Confirm: no email gate, or say what is asked.] Thank you for your time, and for writing that sentence.

भाग 1: स्वागत भाषण
(स्वच्छता जागरूकता कार्यक्रम, [महाविद्यालय का नाम], गया)

सम्मानित मुख्य अतिथि, जिलाधिकारी, गया, श्री/श्रीमती [जिलाधिकारी का नाम] जी;
विशिष्ट अतिथि, हमारे महाविद्यालय के प्राचार्य, श्री/श्रीमती [प्राचार्य का नाम] जी;
कार्यक्रम की अध्यक्षता कर रहे [विश्वविद्यालय का नाम] के प्रतिनिधि, श्री/श्रीमती [अध्यक्ष का नाम] जी;
मंच पर विराजमान अन्य गणमान्य अतिथिगण, आदरणीय शिक्षकगण, मीडिया के साथियो और मेरे प्रिय विद्यार्थियो।

नमस्कार। आप सभी का हार्दिक स्वागत।

आज हमारे बीच मुख्य अतिथि के रूप में जिले के प्रशासनिक प्रमुख, श्री/श्रीमती [जिलाधिकारी का नाम] जी उपस्थित हैं। जिले की स्वच्छता व्यवस्था की ज़िम्मेदारी जिन कंधों पर है, उनका हमारे विद्यार्थियों के बीच आना इस अभियान को शासन और युवाओं से जोड़ता है। हम आपका हृदय से स्वागत करते हैं। कृपया तालियों के साथ उनका अभिनंदन कीजिए।

हमारे विशिष्ट अतिथि, महाविद्यालय के प्राचार्य श्री/श्रीमती [प्राचार्य का नाम] जी, इस आयोजन की प्रेरणा और संबल रहे हैं। आपके मार्गदर्शन में यह परिसर विद्यार्थियों के लिए सीखने के साथ-साथ ज़िम्मेदारी निभाने की जगह भी बना है। आपका स्वागत है। तालियों के साथ अभिनंदन कीजिए।

आज की अध्यक्षता [विश्वविद्यालय का नाम] के प्रतिनिधि श्री/श्रीमती [अध्यक्ष का नाम] जी कर रहे हैं। आपकी उपस्थिति इस कार्यक्रम को शैक्षणिक गरिमा देती है। आपका हार्दिक स्वागत है। कृपया तालियों से अभिनंदन कीजिए।

अब आज के आयोजन का उद्देश्य। स्वच्छता केवल सफ़ाई का काम नहीं है, यह रोज़ की आदत है। यह आदत घर से, मोहल्ले से और कॉलेज के हर कोने से शुरू होती है। आज हम इस जिला-स्तरीय कार्यक्रम में यही संकल्प दोहराएँगे कि गया को स्वच्छ रखने में हर विद्यार्थी अपनी भूमिका निभाएगा। कार्यक्रम में [कार्यक्रम की रूपरेखा: जैसे संबोधन, शपथ, संवाद या पोस्टर प्रदर्शनी, आयोजकों से पुष्टि करें] शामिल हैं।

हम एक बार फिर मंच के सभी अतिथियों और यहाँ उपस्थित हर साथी का स्वागत करते हैं। हमारी कोशिश रहेगी कि कार्यक्रम समय पर शुरू हो और समय पर संपन्न हो। अब मंच संचालक से अनुरोध है कि वे कार्यक्रम को आगे बढ़ाएँ।

धन्यवाद।

भाग 2: धन्यवाद ज्ञापन

माननीय मुख्य अतिथि, जिलाधिकारी, गया, श्री/श्रीमती [जिलाधिकारी का नाम] जी;
विशिष्ट अतिथि, प्राचार्य श्री/श्रीमती [प्राचार्य का नाम] जी;
अध्यक्ष महोदय/महोदया, श्री/श्रीमती [अध्यक्ष का नाम] जी;
मंच पर उपस्थित अन्य गणमान्य अतिथिगण, शिक्षकगण, मीडिया के साथियो और प्रिय विद्यार्थियो।

आज के इस स्वच्छता जागरूकता कार्यक्रम के समापन पर हम आप सभी के प्रति कृतज्ञता व्यक्त करते हैं।

सबसे पहले हमारे मुख्य अतिथि, जिलाधिकारी, गया, श्री/श्रीमती [जिलाधिकारी का नाम] जी का आभार। अपने संबोधन में आपने कहा, "[मुख्य अतिथि के भाषण की एक पंक्ति, कार्यक्रम के दौरान सुनकर भरें]"। यह बात आज यहाँ बैठे हर विद्यार्थी के लिए एक काम की सीख है। हम इसे अपने परिसर और अपने मोहल्ले में उतारेंगे। समय निकालकर आने के लिए हम आपके आभारी हैं।

हमारे विशिष्ट अतिथि, प्राचार्य श्री/श्रीमती [प्राचार्य का नाम] जी का धन्यवाद। आपके सहयोग और मार्गदर्शन के बिना यह आयोजन संभव नहीं था। [प्राचार्य की किसी बात का एक संदर्भ, कार्यक्रम के दौरान भरें।]

कार्यक्रम की अध्यक्षता के लिए श्री/श्रीमती [अध्यक्ष का नाम] जी का हम हृदय से धन्यवाद करते हैं। आपके अध्यक्षीय संदेश ने कार्यक्रम को सार्थक दिशा दी।

इस आयोजन को सफल बनाने में कई हाथ लगे हैं। हम आयोजन समिति के सभी सदस्यों, स्वयंसेवकों और शिक्षकगण का धन्यवाद करते हैं, जिन्होंने तैयारी में दिन-रात मेहनत की। महाविद्यालय के शिक्षकेतर कर्मचारियों को धन्यवाद, जिन्होंने परिसर की सफ़ाई और व्यवस्था सँभाली। ध्वनि और तकनीकी टीम को धन्यवाद, जिनके कारण हर आवाज़ आप तक पहुँची। मीडिया के साथियों को धन्यवाद, जो इस संदेश को समाज तक ले जाएँगे। और आप सभी विद्यार्थियों को धन्यवाद, जो धैर्य के साथ पूरे कार्यक्रम में बने रहे।

आज की सीख को केवल आज तक सीमित न रखें। अपने घर पहुँचकर, अपनी गली में, अपने साथियों के बीच इसे दोहराइए।

कामना है कि गया स्वच्छ रहे और हम सब स्वस्थ रहें।
[यदि कार्यक्रम में हो: अब राष्ट्रगान के लिए सभी से खड़े होने का अनुरोध है।]

धन्यवाद। जय हिंद।

4-email welcome series for a Coimbatore D2C brand of cold-pressed cooking oils, triggered by a 10%-off newsletter sign-up; audience: home cooks aged 28-50 in South Indian metros; English; each email with subject, preview text, an 80-180-word body, one CTA and an unsubscribe line; email 1 delivers the code, email 4 answers 'why pay more than supermarket oil' with claims the brand can prove; goal: first order within 10 days.
Writer note: Bodies are 92, 150, 116 and 163 words; send gaps day 0, 2, 4, 6. Placeholders for every fact the brief does not supply: [Brand], [CODE], offer expiry (same in all four), sender name, founder name, year and story, pressing method, batch size, what the bottle contains, lab report and certificate references, prices (Rs per litre and the supermarket price with date and source), ml per day, customer review, returns policy, postal address and unsubscribe link. Email 4 uses no health claim: it lists three provable things (method, contents, batch traceability) and a per-day cost to be computed from the real price. The oil-by-dish guide in email 3 is common culinary guidance flagged to match the real range. Platform checked as email subject line: each of the four subjects, characters and --field words, all OK (the 3-punctuation and 1-emoji limits checked by hand: none). Gmail clipping not checked: no HTML file exists yet.
samples.text:
WELCOME SERIES: [Brand] cold-pressed cooking oils, Coimbatore
Trigger: newsletter sign-up with a 10% code. Sender name: [Founder first name] at [Brand]. Send gaps: email 1 at once, then day 2, day 4 and day 6. Every email carries the footer below. The offer expiry, if any, is [expiry date, same in all four emails].

EMAIL 1: delivers the code (send immediately)
Subject: Your 10% code is inside
Preview text: Use [CODE] on your first order. Here's what we'll send next.

Welcome to [Brand], and thank you for signing up.

Your code: [CODE]
It takes 10% off your first order. [Expiry date, if any.]

Here's what to expect from us. Over the next week you'll get three short emails: how we started, which oil suits which dish, and an honest answer to "why does cold-pressed oil cost more?" After that, one note a month at most. [Confirm frequency.]

If you ever want to ask us something, just reply to this email. A real person at [Brand] reads it.

CTA: Shop cold-pressed oils with [CODE]

[Footer: [Brand], [postal address], Coimbatore. You're getting this because you signed up on our website. Unsubscribe: [link]]

EMAIL 2: why us (day 2)
Subject: How [Brand] began in Coimbatore
Preview text: One smell, and a kitchen question we couldn't leave alone.

Open a bottle of unrefined oil and the first thing you notice is the smell. It smells of the seed it came from: toasty for sesame, nutty for groundnut.

That smell is the reason [Brand] exists. [Founder name] started it in Coimbatore in [year] because [one true reason, one concrete detail: who, where, what they tasted or cooked]. [Add a second true line only if you can show it.]

So we keep it simple. We press [oils] [pressing method, exactly as on the pack], in [batch size, from your records]. Nothing goes into the bottle except [what it contains, if true: the oil].

You won't find a long list of promises here. You'll find a bottle with a batch code on it, and an oil that smells like food.

Next time, we'll tell you which oil to use for which dish. Until then, cook something you love.

CTA: Browse our oils

[Footer: [Brand], [postal address], Coimbatore. Unsubscribe: [link]]

EMAIL 3: help them choose (day 4)
Subject: Which oil for which dish
Preview text: A quick guide, and one tiny first-win for tonight.

Not sure which bottle to pick? Here's a quick guide. [Match this list to your actual range.]

Sesame (gingelly) oil: tadka, idli podi, pickles. It gives the dish its aroma.
Groundnut oil: dosa, poriyal, everyday sauteing.
Coconut oil: coastal curries and anything that wants a hint of sweetness.
For deep frying, check the smoke point note on the bottle. [Add from your lab sheet.]

A first-win tip for tonight: skip the pan. Warm some rice, add a spoon of sesame oil and a little idli podi, and mix. That's your oil test. If you can smell it before you taste it, it's working.

Pick one bottle first. You can always add more.

CTA: Choose your first oil

[Footer: [Brand], [postal address], Coimbatore. Unsubscribe: [link]]

EMAIL 4: proof and objections (day 6)
Subject: Why our oil costs more than the supermarket's
Preview text: The honest answer, with the paperwork to back it.

Yes, our oil costs more than the oil on a supermarket shelf. A litre of ours is Rs [price]; a typical supermarket litre is Rs [price, with the date and where you checked it]. You deserve the reason.

Here's what the extra pays for, and what we can show:
- How it's made: [pressing method]. Our batch report: [lab report reference].
- What's in the bottle: [oil only, if true]. Certificate: [certificate or licence reference].
- Where it came from: the batch code on the bottle matches [test report or QR page].

And a number you can check: at [N] ml a day, one litre lasts about [N] days, which comes to Rs [X] a day.

"[Customer review: first name, city, one line, verified.]"

If it isn't for you, [returns policy, in plain words: what you can return, within how many days, who pays the shipping].

Your 10% code is still waiting: [CODE]. [Expiry date, if any.]

CTA: Use [CODE] on your first order

[Footer: [Brand], [postal address], Coimbatore. Unsubscribe: [link]]

samples.brief:
Three WhatsApp Channel posts for a Jaipur city-news startup during a monsoon week: a waterlogging traffic alert with diversions (roads as [placeholders]), a poll asking which ward needs drain cleaning first, and a link post to the day's explainer; Hinglish (Roman); each 20-60 words; bold lead line and one action; no reply requests; goal: react, vote or tap the link.
Writer note: Posts are 42, 42 and 28 words, each checked from its own file against plat:whatsapp_message (4,096 characters, no fail). Placeholders: [Road A-D], [time], the source handle for the alert, the ward names, the explainer's one-line finding with its source, reading time and both links. The alert names its source and time so a wrong alert can be traced; the poll promises a result 'kal subah isi channel par' which the newsroom must confirm it can keep. One action per post: tap the live-update link, vote, tap the explainer link. No reply, comment or DM asks, no hashtags; one emoji only. The poll's options sit in the post text for the sample; in the channel they are the poll's options.

samples.brief:
Seven good-morning suvichar forwards (one per weekday) for a Varanasi senior-citizens' yoga group's WhatsApp broadcast list; Hindi in Devanagari; each 15-40 words with one original thought on health, patience or family (no quotes attributed to famous people), at most two emoji, and the sender line '- गंगा तट योग समूह, वाराणसी'; goal: members read them and forward with the sender line intact.
Writer note: Seven separate messages, Monday to Sunday, each 31 to 38 words including the weekday label and sender line, one 🙏 each. Themes: health (breath, walking, thanking the body), patience (ghat steps, the Ganga), family (a phone call, five minutes over chai). All lines are original: no attributed quotes, no medical claims (breathing, walking and posture are suggestions, not treatments), no chain pressure. Each message was checked from its own file and passes. The combined file fails only the lint's caps written for a single message (120 words, 4 emoji); the seven messages together are 231 words and 7 emoji by design.

सोमवार
सुप्रभात 🙏 सोमवार का पहला काम: तीन गहरी साँसें। नाक से धीरे भरिए, मुँह से धीरे छोड़िए। फिर चाय पीजिए, बिना किसी जल्दी के।
- गंगा तट योग समूह, वाराणसी

मंगलवार
सुप्रभात 🙏 जो काम आज नहीं हुआ, वह कल हो जाएगा। घाट की सीढ़ियाँ एक साथ नहीं चढ़ी जातीं, एक-एक करके चढ़ी जाती हैं। आज बस एक सीढ़ी चढ़िए।
- गंगा तट योग समूह, वाराणसी

बुधवार
सुप्रभात 🙏 आज अपने किसी बच्चे या पोते-पोती को फ़ोन कीजिए। काम की बात नहीं, बस यह पूछिए कि खाना खाया या नहीं। यह सवाल बहुत दूर तक पहुँचता है।
- गंगा तट योग समूह, वाराणसी

गुरुवार
सुप्रभात 🙏 सुबह की सैर का नियम सीधा है: जितना चल सकें, उतना चलिए, किसी से तुलना मत कीजिए। आपके घुटनों की अपनी चाल है, उसका सम्मान कीजिए।
- गंगा तट योग समूह, वाराणसी

शुक्रवार
सुप्रभात 🙏 गंगा जी को कभी जल्दी नहीं होती, फिर भी वे हर दिन सागर की ओर बढ़ती हैं। धीरज का मतलब रुकना नहीं, अपनी चाल से चलना है।
- गंगा तट योग समूह, वाराणसी

शनिवार
सुप्रभात 🙏 आज घर में किसी एक के साथ बैठकर पाँच मिनट चाय पीजिए। फ़ोन दूर रखिए। परिवार को आपकी सलाह से पहले आपका साथ चाहिए।
- गंगा तट योग समूह, वाराणसी

रविवार
सुप्रभात 🙏 आज शरीर को धन्यवाद कहिए। उन हाथों को, जो अब भी काम करते हैं। उन पैरों को, जो अब भी चलते हैं। फिर चटाई बिछाइए और आसन कीजिए।
- गंगा तट योग समूह, वाराणसी

Reconciling UPI Collections at Scale for Mid-Size Indian NBFCs

Why matching on loan number and amount stops working as volumes grow, and what a reconciliation process must do instead

White paper | [Company name] | [Month Year] | For CFOs and heads of operations

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Mid-size non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) now collect a growing share of EMIs through the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) [source needed: NPCI monthly UPI statistics for the latest month]. The channels include payment links, dynamic QR codes, static QR codes at field points, in-app payments and recurring mandates [source needed: NBFC collection mix]. Each channel produces its own record of a payment, with its own identifier, its own status and its own timing. The loan management system (LMS) holds a fourth record, keyed to the loan account.

Reconciliation is the work of proving that these records describe the same money. At low volumes a finance team does this in spreadsheets, and it works. At scale, three things break it. Records cannot be matched on a single reliable key. Payments sit in states that are neither success nor failure. And settlement reaches the bank account in batches, days after the customer has paid.

The cost goes beyond the reconciliation team's hours. A borrower who has paid is still called by a collections agent. An overdue status is wrong when it reaches the credit bureau. Month-end close waits on open items. Audit questions take days to answer [source needed: figures on the cost of reconciliation breaks, if the paper is to quantify this].

This paper makes one argument. Spreadsheet reconciliation, gateway reports, LMS-native modules and in-house matching scripts each solve part of the problem and fail at a predictable point. A process that holds at scale matches on several keys and tracks every payment through its states until settlement. It treats unmatched items as a queue with owners and ageing, not as a monthly clean-up. The sections that follow set out the problem and compare the common approaches fairly. The full paper ends with a checklist that a finance head can use to test any approach, including one built in-house.

THE PROBLEM

How a UPI collection actually travels

A borrower pays Rs 4,250 towards an EMI due on the 5th. The payment link was sent by SMS. She pays at 11:52 pm on the due date, from a UPI app, to a virtual payment address linked to the NBFC's collection account.

The payment aggregator marks the transaction as successful within seconds. The NBFC's app shows "Payment received". But the money has not reached the NBFC's bank account. It arrives the next working day, in a settlement file with several hundred other transactions, net of any fees. [Confirm settlement timing with the aggregator and bank; source needed.] The bank statement shows one credit line. The LMS posts the receipt on the 7th, after an operations user uploads the settlement file.

On the 6th, the collections team calls her. She has paid, and she is, correctly, annoyed.

This scenario is illustrative, not a client case. Every element of it is routine.

Why the records do not line up

A single UPI collection leaves at least four records.

First, the aggregator's order record, with its own order identifier and a status. Second, the UPI transaction record, with the bank reference number, often called the UTR or RRN. Third, the bank statement line, which carries the settlement, often one line for many payments. Fourth, the LMS receipt, keyed to the loan account number.

These records use different identifiers, different cut-off times and different status vocabularies. The loan account number, the only key the NBFC controls, is rarely carried reliably through the payment rail. Customers type remarks by hand. Some payments come from a family member's UPI handle, not the borrower's.

Five failure patterns follow, and each is common.

- Pending or deemed-success payments that settle later, or reverse.
- Partial payments, and payments that cover two EMIs at once.
- Duplicate payments from a customer who retries.
- Third-party payments, where the payer's name does not match the borrower's.
- Refunds, reversals and disputes that reach the bank file weeks after the original credit [verify the dispute timelines and the process under NPCI's dispute framework].

What it costs

Four costs recur in NBFC finance and operations teams.

Customer experience. A borrower who has paid but is chased loses trust, and the call may breach the NBFC's own fair-practice commitments [verify against the RBI Fair Practices Code and the NBFC's board-approved policy].

Credit reporting. A payment posted late can leave the account showing overdue when the customer has paid. NBFCs report to credit information companies at a fixed frequency under RBI directions [verify: current reporting frequency and effective date]. An error that sits unresolved across two reporting cycles can reach the borrower's bureau record.

Close and audit. Month-end close waits on unmatched items. Auditors ask for the trail from bank credit to loan receipt, and the answer should not take a day to assemble.

Team time. Finance and operations staff spend a share of every month matching rows by hand [source needed: hours or headcount, from a client or a survey].

Why scale changes the nature of the problem

At a few hundred payments a month, a spreadsheet and a careful analyst absorb all of this. At lakhs of payments a month, three things change.

Volume turns exceptions into a stream. If a small percentage of payments fails to match automatically, that small percentage is still a daily queue [source needed: observed unmatched rates, if available].

Variety multiplies. Each new collection channel, aggregator and bank adds its own file format, its own cut-off and its own error codes.

Time stretches. The gap between a customer paying and the NBFC knowing it has been paid widens at the point where the business most needs it to close.

For a mid-size NBFC, defined here as one in the RBI's Middle Layer under Scale Based Regulation [verify definition and threshold], these pressures arrive before the finance team has grown to match them.

WHY CURRENT APPROACHES FALL SHORT

Most NBFCs use one or more of four approaches. Each is rational. Each works within a range.

1. Spreadsheet reconciliation

What it does well. It is cheap, flexible and fully understood by the person who built it. For a single channel and low volume, it is the right tool.

Where it breaks. Matching is by lookup on one or two columns, so a payment that arrives with a mistyped loan number, or one payment covering two loans, falls out. File size and row limits slow it down. Version control is weak, so an auditor cannot easily see who changed what. And it is retrospective: breaks are found at month-end.

2. Aggregator and bank reports

What it does well. These reports are authoritative for their own channel. Settlement files from an aggregator show exactly what was paid out, and bank statements are the record of money received.

Where it breaks. Each report covers only its own channel and uses its own format. None knows the loan account. Reconciling across three aggregators and two banks means three formats to align by hand, and the NBFC still has to map each payment to a loan.

3. LMS-native reconciliation modules

What it does well. The LMS knows the loan, the due amount and the schedule. Posting a receipt and updating the overdue status are its core strengths, and a module built into it keeps one source of truth for the loan.

Where it breaks. Most LMS modules work on uploaded batch files. They have little visibility of the payment's state between the customer's tap and the bank's settlement, so pending, reversed and duplicate payments surface late. Adding a new aggregator often needs a vendor change request.

4. In-house matching scripts

What it does well. An engineering team can encode the NBFC's own rules exactly, and control the data. For firms with strong data engineering, this is a legitimate choice.

Where it breaks. The scripts must keep pace with changes in aggregator file layouts, bank formats and UPI rules. The knowledge often sits with one or two people. Exceptions usually end in a spreadsheet anyway, because the tool has no queue, ownership or ageing for unmatched items.

What the four approaches have in common

Laid side by side, the four approaches share three limits.

They match on weak keys. Loan number plus amount is the usual rule. It fails when the loan number is wrong, missing or shared.

They see money at one moment, not through time. A payment is treated as matched or unmatched, not as an item moving through initiation, success, settlement and posting.

They treat exceptions as someone's problem. A break is found, fixed in a sheet and forgotten. There is no queue, no owner and no ageing report that a CFO can read.

A reconciliation process that holds at scale has to fix these three things. What that process looks like, and how to test it, is the subject of the remaining sections.

WHAT FOLLOWS IN THE FULL PAPER (outline)

The approach. A vendor-neutral framework with three parts: multi-key matching, a payment lifecycle ledger from initiation to LMS posting, and an exceptions queue with owners and ageing. A description in words of the data flow follows, with what each step needs.

Evidence. One documented case or pilot, with consent and sourced numbers [client result: to be supplied and permissioned].

Evaluation checklist. Questions a CFO can put to any vendor or internal team: which keys are matched, how pending and reversed payments are handled, how long a break stays open, and what the audit trail shows.

Conclusion and next step. A request for a working session or demo, with a short company description at the end.

References.

[1] NPCI, UPI product statistics, [month and year], [link]. [source needed]
[2] RBI, Scale Based Regulation: A Revised Regulatory Framework for NBFCs, [date], [link]. [verify]
[3] RBI directions on credit information reporting, [date], [link]. [verify]
[4] RBI, Fair Practices Code for NBFCs, [date], [link]. [verify]
